transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2025-07-22 15:00 PDT
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (Cascade Head of ML), Tom Baker (CTO), Sofia Martinez (Platform), Aaron Li (SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery focusing on cost/unit economics across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer provided volume ranges and budget constraints; team asked about batching, KV caching hit rates, model quantization tradeoffs, and expected unit costs. Agreed next steps: share pricing examples, security docs, run short benchmark.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes. quick intros, then dive into your current stack and what you're trying to optimize for.
[00:18] Evelyn: Hi all, Evelyn here. we run a customer support augmentation product—real time chat summarization and suggestion. average request length is short, but we have spikes. our main constraint is cost per active user, we're trying to keep model cost under a predictable budget.
[00:36] Tom: Tom here. We care about latency under 300ms p50 for short prompts, and overall token spend monthly is... roughly in the 200M token range today but could grow to 1B in six months if we hit product-market fit.
[00:51] Jordan: thanks. Priya from our SE team will help with the deeper perf questions. first, high level — do you have a preference for hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[01:03] Sofia: We prefer hosted for initial pilot to move fast, but we have procurement limits above $X/month and for scale we'll likely need dedicated for capacity predictability and maybe private for compliance if we hit enterprise sales.
[01:18] Priya: ok. for economics, there are a few levers: per-token pricing (hosted), batching to increase GPU throughput, and prefix/KV caching to avoid re-generating repeated context. also quantization and model variants — cheaper, smaller models for lower-latency, lower-cost routes.
[01:36] Aaron: can you quantify savings from batching & caching?
[01:41] Priya: rough numbers — batching can improve throughput and lower per-token compute cost by around 20-40% depending on request size and sequence length; prefix/KV caching depends heavily on hit rate — if you get 30-50% prefix hit rate on common prompts, you could cut effective output token compute by similar amounts because you're not recomputing the prefix. these are illustrative; we'll need your trace to estimate.
[02:05] Evelyn: when you say per-token pricing on hosted — what numbers are we looking at?
[02:10] Jordan: we typically show examples in the pricing sheet, but ballpark for hosted generation workloads is in the low fractions of a cent per thousand tokens — apologies some of our public numbers vary — but for demos we show $X per 1k output tokens as an example. more importantly, the combination of batching, caching, and model choice moves effective unit cost.
[02:30] Tom: we want concrete dollar comparisons: hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved capacity amortized cost.
[02:35] Priya: right. Dedicated changes the math: you pay committed GPU capacity monthly — for steady high volume, dedicated can be materially cheaper per token because you're amortizing the hardware. example: if you commit a V100-equivalent pool, your monthly committed spend might be in the low tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands depending on size; divide by tokens served to get amortized cost. The hosted per-token is simpler but can be higher for sustained large volume.
[02:58] Sofia: any rules of thumb about break-even volume where dedicated becomes cheaper?
[03:03] Priya: rule-of-thumb: once you're consistently doing several hundred million output tokens a month and have predictable load, dedicated tends to beat hosted. but it depends a lot on caching & batching — if you can get high cache hit rates, hosted looks better longer. we'll run numbers once we have your token distribution.
[03:25] [03:25] Speaker 1: quick question — how about cold starts and latency with dedicated vs hosted?
[03:31] Priya: Dedicated gives you control over pinned instances and capacity so you avoid cold starts; hosted has warmed pools and burst capacity but if you need strict p50/p95 SLOs, dedicated or pinned instances are safer.
[03:42] Evelyn: you mentioned quantization — how much accuracy hit should we expect if we go 8-bit or 4-bit? our NLU requires pretty high fidelity for suggestions.
[03:50] Priya: 8-bit quant is often a great sweet spot — minimal quality impact for big compute savings. 4-bit can be trickier and model-dependent; we typically recommend running a small eval suite — Redwood Optimize can give model/quant suggestions based on your eval set.
[04:06] Tom: could you walk through a sample calculation? like for a 1k token response average, what does the cost look like hosted vs dedicated?
[04:14] Jordan: sure. illustrative example — assume hosted price of $0.8 per 1M output tokens (example only) — that's $0.0008 per token. 1k token response ~ $0.80. with batching you may amortize request overhead so effective cost could drop 20% to ~$0.64 per 1k. with 40% cache hits on prefixes maybe further reduces average. Dedicated: say committed pool amortized to $20k/month serving 500M tokens -> $0.00004 per token -> $0.04 per 1k. obviously numbers vary; this is just to show orders of magnitude.
[04:56] Sofia: that dedicated number seems orders different — $0.04 vs $0.64 per 1k is huge. what's driving that gap?
[05:03] Priya: the committed GPU amortization in the example assumed high utilization; the dedicated figure only makes sense at high utilization. if your load is spiky or low, the amortized number worsens. also dedicated requires ops overhead and longer procurement.
[05:18] Aaron: procurement note — if we go dedicated, what's the minimum term?
[05:22] Jordan: typical Dedicated commitments are monthly or annual with discounts for longer terms and larger pools. we can send your account rep options in the pricing sheet.
[05:30] [06:05] Evelyn: what about caching mechanics — is the KV cache shared across requests or per-tenant? we need isolation.
[06:12] Priya: good point. for Hosted we have customer-scoped KV caching; for Dedicated we can offer per-tenant caches or dedicated kernels — isolation options are configurable. on private deployments you manage it entirely. beware of prefix cache warmup: first few requests have no cache.
[06:30] Tom: curious about fallback behavior — if dedicated capacity spikes, do you spill to hosted?
[06:35] Jordan: yes — smart routing supports fallback policies. you can set primary as Dedicated and fallback to Hosted or a lower-capacity model. fallback can be automatic to keep availability.
[06:44] [07:12] Sofia: any tooling to help simulate cost with different cache hit rates and batching?
[07:18] Priya: we have Redwood Optimize that generates suggestions and can simulate effective unit costs across scenarios given your token distribution; we also provide example CSV-based calculators. we'll share a starter template.
[07:28] [09:05] Evelyn: assume we want to cap spend at $15k/month for pilot — how many active users can we support at certain latencies?
[09:13] Jordan: need traffic profile — if avg 1k tokens per session and avg 2 sessions/day per active user, that's 2k tokens per user/day => ~60k tokens/month per user. at $0.0008/token hosted, that's about $48/month per user, so $15k would cover ~312 users. but caching/batching can lower that. again numbers illustrative.
[09:45] Tom: we'll share real traces so you can run the calc.
[09:50] Aaron: about encryption — do you support customer-managed keys?
[09:54] Priya: yes, Hosted supports KMS integrations for encrypt-at-rest keys and TLS in transit; Dedicated and Private can integrate with your KMS or HSM. we'll include the security doc.
[10:05] [11:22] Speaker 1: I heard you mention regression alerts — can Redwood detect quality drops after switching quantization or models?
[11:29] Priya: Redwood Optimize and our eval hooks let you run prompt sets and surface regressions. you can set alert thresholds and tie them into rollouts — automatic rollback if metrics degrade.
[11:45] Evelyn: procurement will ask for SOC2 and ISO — do you have certs?
[11:50] Jordan: yes, SOC 2 in progress or already done — we'll attach the compliance pack. (minor audio overlap)
[12:05] [13:00] Tom: for the benchmark run — can you run using our prompts and measure P50/P95 and tokens per response?
[13:07] Priya: yes, we can run a controlled benchmark on Hosted or Dedicated; SE-run on hosted is quickest. we'll share benchmarking scripts.
[13:20] Sofia: what about partial responses and streaming — does that add cost?
[13:25] Priya: cost is token-based; streaming reduces latency but token count is the metric. streaming can slightly increase overhead if you break responses into many small chunks, but usually negligible.
[13:40] [15:02] Jordan: quick note on pricing complexity: per-token price is simplest to compare, but your effective cost is tokens * per-token + infra amortization + any caching/batching gains. We'll model scenarios after you share traces.
[15:25] Evelyn: ok. what would you consider the lowest-risk pilot for us?
[15:30] Jordan: start hosted pilot with conservative rate limits and enabled KV caching + batching suggestions, run for 2-4 weeks; measure cache hit & latency; if usage is stable, consider dedicated commit. that way you avoid procurement friction.
[15:45] Aaron: On the topic of token accounting — do you show token-level breakdowns by route/model in the console?
[15:52] Priya: yes, Console provides per-route and per-model token breakdowns, cost attribution, and traces. you can export CSVs for finance.
[16:08] [18:00] Sofia: will you share an example of a dedicated commitment and how you amortize GPUs? we want to compare apples-to-apples.
[18:05] Jordan: yes, we'll include amortization examples in the pricing sheet — GPU equivalent, utilization assumptions, and headroom for bursts.
[18:22] [21:10] Evelyn: any hidden costs we should plan for? network egress? monitoring retention fees?
[21:18] Jordan: potential extras: long-term logs/metrics retention, advanced observability add-ons, and private network egress if you use Private deployment with dedicated connectivity. we'll call them out in the sheet.
[21:40] Tom: last specific question — how do you measure batching benefits? is it request count vs token count?
[21:46] Priya: we measure throughput (tokens/sec) and GPU utilization. batching helps when many small requests can be combined to fill GPU compute. effective per-token cost is tokens served divided by GPU-seconds consumed — batching increases tokens per GPU-second.
[22:05] [26:00] (conversation drift + some crosstalk while sharing a doc link)
[26:30] Jordan: OK, to recap next steps — we'll send pricing + security docs, SE will run a hosted benchmark using the traces you provide, and we'll schedule a 45-minute deep dive on batching/caching with your SREs.
[26:45] Evelyn: sounds good. Sofia will coordinate the traces.
[26:50] Sofia: yep will upload to the shared folder and ping you.
[27:00] Aaron: procurement questions we'll defer till after the pilot.
[27:08] Jordan: great. any other blockers?
[27:12] Tom: timeline — we want to run pilot within two weeks.
[27:15] Jordan: we can target week of 2025-07-28 for the benchmark and pilot.
[27:22] [44:40] (closing pleasantries, small audio overlap, agreement on dates)
[44:54] Jordan: thanks everyone. action items as noted — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the pricing sheet.

References shared: pricing sheet (link: https://redwood.example/papers/pricing-sample), security pack (note: SOC2 summary + KMS notes attached), benchmark script template (link: shared drive /redwood/benchmarks/cascade-sample.zip).
